case_study_insert.main_stem: Carrick Shelf Analytics (CSA) is a private limited company in the retail technology (IoT) sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2017 by Matteo Ricci, the business supplies smart-shelf sensor systems to national supermarket chains and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. CSA plans to invest $950,000 in a new computer-vision smart-shelf platform with recyclable sensor housings, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $340,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.50 a unit and a selling price of $26.50, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. CSA faces two operational problems: field-technician absenteeism has reached 8% and labour turnover is rising, while quality complaints about inaccurate stock alerts are increasing.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: The smart-shelf rollout covered 140 supermarket stores, and 2.6 million shelf-scan events were recorded last quarter. Out-of-stock incidents fell 31% in pilot stores. The field-sensor defect rate is 2.6%, down from 4.4% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 46 to 24 per month. Market research of 700 store managers found 71% would pay $0.15 more per shelf per month for real-time alerts, and 48% cite stock accuracy as their top priority. A training needs analysis shows 15 of 38 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new calibrated mounting kits; off-the-job training courses at the regional college cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Carrick Shelf Analytics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.9% to 5.6%, the third rise this year, increasing costs for variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage rises 5.4% from $13.10 to $13.81 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills for field and warehouse staff. (3) Semiconductor and shelf-sensor component costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year and grocery price inflation is 7.2%, while consumer spending on grocery own-label goods grew 4.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: CSA plans to part-finance its computer-vision smart-shelf expansion through a $600,000 bank loan rather than retained profit alone. Explain two advantages for CSA of raising the $600,000 through a bank loan rather than using all $350,000 of retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A ten-year bank loan spreads the cost of the $950,000 expansion across the working life of the computer-vision smart-shelf platform instead of draining CSA's cash reserves at once. Keeping part of the $350,000 retained profit inside the business preserves a liquidity buffer to absorb the 9.8% rise in semiconductor and shelf-sensor component costs without breaching supermarket supply agreements or delaying the 140-store rollout.

Point 2: Fixed equal repayments make the $600,000 debt predictable, so CSA can budget its cash flow precisely alongside fixed costs of $340,000 a year and interest payable, which rose from $55,000 to $78,000. Because the loan is external debt rather than new share capital, Matteo Ricci retains full ownership and control of the private limited company; no outside investor gains voting rights, and the flat laissez-faire structure can continue without shareholder interference in day-to-day decisions about the 38 employees and the sensor platform.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Carrick Shelf Analytics and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: CSA is launching its computer-vision smart-shelf platform to national supermarket chains. Consider a stand at the National Grocery Retail Expo, targeted LinkedIn advertising aimed at grocery procurement managers, or sponsorship of a food-industry trade podcast. Which should CSA choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National Grocery Retail Expo: A stand at the expo would put CSA in front of hundreds of supermarket buyers in person, allowing live demonstrations of calibrated mounting kits and the 31% fall in out-of-stock incidents recorded in pilot stores. Face-to-face meetings build trust quickly for a private limited company asking chains to pay $0.15 more per shelf per month. However, stand fees, travel and staff time are expensive, the audience is broad rather than targeted, and much of it will never place an order, so cost per qualified lead is high for a 38-employee business funding a $950,000 expansion.

Targeted LinkedIn advertising: LinkedIn lets CSA aim its message precisely at procurement managers in national supermarket chains, exactly the audience whose behaviour its research of 700 store managers measured. The 71% who would pay $0.15 more per shelf and the 48% who cite stock accuracy as their top priority can be targeted by job title and sector, with measurable click-through rates and retargeting of warm leads. Drawbacks are that LinkedIn ads require ongoing budget and creative effort, and senior buyers may ignore generic adverts unless they are backed by case-study proof.

Food-industry trade podcast sponsorship: A podcast sponsorship reaches food-retail listeners at low cost and suits CSA's storytelling about its 31% out-of-stock improvement. However, reach is slow to build, measurement of direct sales impact is weak, and listeners may be consumers or suppliers rather than the 700 store managers who control shelf-technology purchasing decisions.

Recommendation: CSA should choose targeted LinkedIn advertising. It reaches the exact procurement-manager audience, is measurable and affordable beside the $950,000 investment, and scales from 140 stores to chains nationwide. The expo is rejected as a costly one-off with poorly targeted footfall, and podcast sponsorship is rejected as too slow and hard to measure for a product launch that must convert the 71% of managers already willing to pay more for real-time alerts.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CSA with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CSA with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the Grocery Retail Expo and the trade podcast are rejected.

questions.question_text: CSA's field-technician absenteeism has reached 8% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for CSA of its laissez-faire leadership style for the software engineers building the new platform.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives CSA's software engineers freedom to design and test code without micromanagement, which suits creative problem-solving such as training the computer-vision models that interpret shelf-scan events. High autonomy satisfies esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow), raising job satisfaction and reducing the risk that skilled developers leave a 38-person business, where losing one of a handful of AI engineers would stall the $950,000 platform launch and repeat the onboarding delays already visible in the field team.

Point 2: Engineers who own their work also generate the most useful ideas for the platform, such as reducing the field-sensor defect rate from 2.6% toward zero, lowering customer complaints. Higher engagement makes attendance reliable — critical when absenteeism has reached 8% — and strengthens the flat structure CSA values, because laissez-faire works only when staff are self-motivated; CSA's low managerial overhead keeps fixed costs at $340,000 a year while still attracting scarce engineers away from larger rivals.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to CSA's leadership style, platform and absenteeism problem.

questions.question_text: CSA must train 15 field technicians to install and calibrate the new calibrated mounting kits across its 140 supermarket stores. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should CSA choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training during live installations is directly matched to the new calibrated mounting kits and CSA's own sensor hardware, costs nothing in course fees, and keeps the 15 technicians productive while the rollout to 140 supermarket stores continues. Given that absenteeism has reached 8% and the sensor defect rate is 2.6%, learning by doing with senior engineers present embeds CSA's exact torque and calibration settings. Drawbacks are that senior engineers teaching the kits lose short-term capacity, bad habits can spread if trainers are inconsistent, and no external certificate is awarded, which may weaken CSA's position when supermarket auditors ask for evidence of competence.

Off-the-job training at the regional college: The college course at $750 per employee gives 15 technicians a recognised certificate and structured instruction, costing $11,250 in total — affordable against the $950,000 expansion. It removes technicians from the rollout for course days, however, and the generic syllabus may not match CSA's calibrated mounting kits, so follow-up coaching on site would still be required before the 140-store rollout completes.

Decision: CSA should choose on-the-job training. It is free of the $11,250 fee, keeps technicians on the 140-store rollout, and targets CSA's specific mounting kits precisely when absenteeism (8%) and the 2.6% defect rate demand immediate, practical improvement. Off-the-job training is rejected as the primary route because removing 15 of 38 staff stalls the rollout and duplicates what in-house seniors can teach; CSA can send two lead technicians to the college afterwards to earn certificates for audit purposes once the rollout stabilises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CSA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of CSA.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of CSA with a well-justified decision covering cost, rollout speed and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CSA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $340,000 ÷ ($26.50 − $18.50) = $340,000 ÷ $8.00 = 42,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 42,500 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $26.50 − $18.50 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CSA's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. CSA's managers can compare the 42,500-unit break-even output with actual output of 60,000 units to confirm the smart-shelf platform is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 17,500 units, before committing to the full $950,000 rollout beyond the 140 stores already live.
2. Contribution per unit of $8.00 lets managers model pricing changes, for example whether a $0.15 per-shelf price rise demanded by supermarket chains would lift contribution to $8.15 and make the 9.8% component-cost inflation absorbable without losing contracts.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $340,000 a year and the $8.00 contribution helps managers test whether retained profit and the $600,000 bank loan can service repayments while the new computer-vision platform ramps up, so over-extension of the private limited company is avoided.
4. Managers can use unit-cost data ($340,000 ÷ 60,000 units + $18.50 = $24.17 a unit) to benchmark kit costs across quarters, identify where the 2.6% defect rate and 24 monthly complaints consume margin, and press suppliers on the 9.8% rise in semiconductor costs.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 42,500 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: the 17,500-unit margin of safety against 60,000 units confirms headroom; contribution per unit of $8.00 supports price and discount modelling; fixed costs of $340,000 and the $600,000 loan are tested for repayment feasibility; and unit costs of $24.17 are benchmarked to attack the 2.6% defect rate and 9.8% component inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CSA's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has CSA's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 19.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 24.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue rose from $4,600,000 in 2024 to $5,200,000 in 2025, an increase of 13.0%. Cost of sales grew more slowly, from $2,760,000 to $2,860,000, so gross profit improved from $1,840,000 to $2,340,000. Operating profit rose from $690,000 to $988,000, an increase of 43.2%, as revenue growth outpaced the cost base. Capital employed grew from $3,450,000 to $4,120,000, a rise of 19.4%, reflecting investment in non-current assets for the rollout. Interest payable rose from $55,000 to $78,000 with higher borrowing, but remains small relative to the profit improvement.

Evaluation: Profitability has strengthened across the board. The gross profit improvement from 40.0% to 45.0% shows CSA is passing on component costs to supermarket customers more effectively, likely through its $0.15 per-shelf premium. The operating improvement from 15.0% to 19.0% shows tight control of fixed costs at $340,000 a year even while scaling from 140 stores. The return on capital employed rose from 20.0% to 24.0%, meaning each dollar of capital generates more profit, though the new $950,000 computer-vision platform will temporarily raise capital employed further before sales ramp up. However, inventory of recurring risks — the 2.6% sensor defect rate, 24 monthly complaints and 8% absenteeism — could erode margins if not fixed, and the 9.8% component-cost inflation will test the 2026 figures.

Conclusion: CSA's financial performance has improved. Every profitability measure moved in the right direction between 2024 and 2025, supported by genuine cost control rather than one-off items. CSA should protect the gains by fixing its quality problems and locking in component supply before the platform investment completes.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue growth, cost control, capital investment and interest movements, and a justified conclusion on whether CSA's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CSA of using recyclable plastic housings in its smart-shelf sensors.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recyclable housings align CSA with the sustainability requirements increasingly written into national supermarket listing agreements, strengthening Matteo Ricci's case for winning contracts for the computer-vision smart-shelf platform across 140 stores and beyond. They also reinforce the premium $0.15 per-shelf positioning, because 71% of the 700 store managers in CSA's research will pay extra for a modern, low-impact offering, and recyclable housings differentiate CSA from rivals competing on price alone.

Disadvantage: Recyclable housings can be less durable than virgin plastic, risking a rise in the field-sensor defect rate from 2.6% and more returns, reinstallation visits and the $750-per-employee-equivalent service burden. They may also cost more per unit than standard housings, adding to the $18.50 variable cost and squeezing CSA's $8.00 contribution per unit at a time when component costs are already rising 9.8% — unless supermarket chains accept a higher price or CSA absorbs the cost as a marketing investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CSA's costs, defect rate, research data and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 4.9% to 5.6%, the 5.4% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in component costs will affect CSA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.9% to 5.6%): If CSA's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.7% rise adds about $4,200 a year to interest costs, modest against interest payable already budgeted into CSA's accounts. Higher rates also raise the cost of any future borrowing beyond the $950,000 expansion and may make supermarket customers more cautious about capital projects, slightly slowing the pace at which stores adopt smart shelves. Management can partly shield CSA by fixing the loan rate at renewal.

Minimum wage increase (5.4%, from $13.10 to $13.81 per hour): With a workforce of 38 concentrated in field installation and warehouse roles, most near the minimum wage, CSA's annual wage base is roughly 38 staff multiplied by about 2,000 hours and $13.10, around $995,600, so a 5.4% rise adds roughly $53,700 a year. That is a significant recurring cash cost for a business with $340,000 fixed costs, and it compounds with the 8% absenteeism problem, because remaining staff may demand overtime premiums.

Component cost inflation (9.8% semiconductors and shelf sensors): CSA's $18.50 variable cost per unit is dominated by sensor hardware, so a 9.8% rise in components implies roughly $1.10–$1.30 of extra cost per unit; at 60,000 units that is about $66,000 to $78,000 a year, directly eroding the $8.00 contribution per unit to around $6.70–$6.90 and raising the break-even output from 42,500 units to roughly 50,000 units. It also weakens the business-case narrative used to justify the $950,000 expansion.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in component costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every one of CSA's 60,000 units sold, totals roughly $66,000 to $78,000 a year, erodes the $8.00 contribution and pushes break-even output upward — threatening the very margin that makes the $950,000 platform viable. The wage rise is the second-largest burden at roughly $53,700, while the interest-rate rise is the smallest and can be managed by fixing the loan; CSA should also negotiate component supply contracts and push for the $0.15 per-shelf premium to pass costs through.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CSA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CSA's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CSA with a well-justified judgement that component-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
